title: Gemma 4 QAT: 4-Bit Weights That Keep Their Quality
hook: Squeezing a model to 4 bits after training loses quality. Quantization-aware training bakes the rounding into training instead — and Google shipped Gemma 4 checkpoints that do exactly that.
key_points: Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates low-precision rounding during training so the model learns to tolerate it.
Result: 4-bit weights with far less quality loss than post-training quantization of the same model.
Google released Gemma 4 QAT collections, including Q4_0 and mobile-targeted variants.
Community builders (Unsloth) published their own QAT versions with KL-divergence analysis vs. the full model.
content_html: Running a large model in 4-bit precision slashes its memory footprint, but the usual route — quantizing a finished model after the fact — throws away quality, sometimes a lot. Quantization-aware training (QAT) takes the opposite approach: it simulates the low-precision rounding during training, so the network learns weights that survive being squeezed down.
extra_html: Google released QAT versions of its open-weights Gemma 4 family, including Q4_0 checkpoints and mobile-targeted variants, so the models run in 4-bit with far less degradation than naive post-training quantization would cause. Because QAT exposes the model to quantization error while it still has a chance to adjust, the 4-bit weights stay much closer to the full-precision model's behavior. The community picked it up quickly: Unsloth published its own QAT builds alongside KL-divergence analysis comparing the quantized outputs to the original. For learners, Gemma 4 QAT is a clean, concrete illustration of why when you quantize matters as much as how much — see the linked collections for the specific sizes and formats.

related.title: Gemma 4: Google DeepMind's Open Multimodal Models
related.hook: An open-weight multimodal family (2.3B-31B) that now thinks before answering and, at 12B, skips separate vision/audio encoders entirely — still small enough for a 16GB laptop.

related.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization
related.hook: Already trained a giant LLM? GPTQ squeezes its weights down to 3–4 bits afterward — no retraining — with surprisingly little quality loss.

related.title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
related.hook: Not all weights are equal - protect the 1% that matter most (flagged by activation magnitude) and quantize the rest to 4-bit with minimal quality loss.

flashcards.prompt: How does quantization-aware training (QAT) differ from post-training quantization?

choices.text: QAT simulates low-precision rounding during training so the model learns to tolerate it
QAT quantizes only after training is fully finished, like other methods
QAT keeps the model in full precision and never reduces bit-width

flashcards.explanation_html: Post-training quantization rounds a finished model's weights and absorbs whatever quality loss results; QAT bakes the rounding into the training loop so the network adapts to it, preserving more quality at low bit-widths.

flashcards.prompt: Why does QAT generally yield better 4-bit quality than post-training quantization?
flashcards.back_html: Because the model sees the quantization error during training and adjusts its weights to compensate, rather than having precision stripped away after the fact.

flashcards.prompt: What did Google release for Gemma 4 under QAT?
flashcards.back_html: QAT checkpoint collections including Q4_0 and mobile-targeted variants, letting the open-weights models run in 4-bit with minimal quality loss.
